summary: Suggests an addressing scheme for using the ISO Connectionless Network Protocol (CLNP) in the Internet, as a solution to a problem with "ISO-grams". It revises RFC 986 and invited discussion.

plainLanguage.summary:
ISO's network layer lets each network choose its own address format, which is a problem when those networks have to route for each other.

This RFC fixes one layout for the Internet: a fixed 20-octet address where the first eight octets identify the routing domain and the rest is left for the domain to fill in as it likes.

questions: how to use clnp addresses in the internet
how are iso addresses used in the internet
how long is an internet clnp address
subtitle: How an ISO network address is laid out so that ISO datagrams can be routed in the Internet.

tldr.problem: ISO's Connectionless-Mode Network Protocol allows a great deal of freedom in how addresses are assigned, and no particular address format had been chosen for use inside the Internet.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1069 fixes a 20-octet NSAP address for the Internet: an AFI of 47, the Internet code designator 0006, a version number, a global area number, a routing domain number, padding, a routing-domain-specific part and a selector for the user protocol.
tldr.outcome: The layout lets each routing domain use its own internal address format while inter-domain routing works from the first eight octets. RFC 1069 revised RFC 986 and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 1069 is a proposed protocol from February 1989 and has not been obsoleted. It revised RFC 986 so that the ISO addressing used in the Internet could also be useful for routing under new inter- and intra-domain routing protocols, and for large numbers of networks and routing domains.

sections.title: Why ISO Addressing in the Internet Needed Rules
sections.content:
The data communications protocols emerging from the international standardization effort warranted early integration into the existing Internet infrastructure. There were two possible approaches. The top-down one integrated ISO applications such as FTAM, X.400 and VTP on top of the transport function of the IP protocol suite. The bottom-up one integrated the whole ISO tower without merging the two suites, which could make use of the fact that ISO-CLNP and IP are very similar in function. That implied a multiprotocol function in some or all of the Internet gateways, with the result that large portions of the Internet, in particular the backbones, could become usable for full implementations of the ISO protocol stack.

A major problem with the bottom-up approach was the open issue of ISO addressing within CLNP. The ISO network layer addressing standard allows a great deal of flexibility in the assignment of addresses, and a particular address format had to be chosen. A further problem was the need for implementation and integration of routing facilities for the ISO-compatible subset of the Internet environment.

The scheme proposed here uses more flexible addresses than those used in the current IP Internet environment. That flexibility lets some routing domains base their internal routing protocol on addresses derived from current IP addresses, lets others base routing on addresses following the intra-domain routing protocol being developed by ANSI and ISO, and leaves room for a future inter-domain routing protocol.

The scheme builds on the concept of routing domains as used by ANSI and ISO. This is similar to, but not identical with, the Internet's autonomous system. Routing domains include a combination of gateways, networks and end systems, not just gateways, and their boundaries may be used to define associated access control and policy routing constraints. Like autonomous systems, they may be assumed to be topologically contiguous. There is no reason in advance why routing domains for the ISO IP need any particular relation to the autonomous systems already assigned for IP. Assigning the specific routing domain identifiers is an assigned numbers function that is beyond the scope of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet and the ISO network layer could be joined up, because both do roughly the same job. The obstacle was addressing: ISO lets each network invent its own address format, and the Internet needs a common one to route between them.

sections.title: Where the Addresses Sit in the CLNP Header
sections.content:
The CLNP is documented elsewhere, but the RFC reproduces an illustration of the CLNP header as Figure 1, because the addressing part of the header is the subject of the document: the source and destination address.

The header is divided into parts. The fixed part carries the network layer protocol identifier in octet 1, the length indicator in octet 2, the version and protocol identifier extension in octet 3, the lifetime in octet 4, the type field with its SP, MS and E/R bits in octet 5, the segment length in octets 6 and 7, and the checksum in octets 8 and 9. The address part follows: the destination address length indicator in octet 10, the destination address in octets 11 through m-1, the source address length indicator in octet m, and the source address in octets m+1 through n-1. The segmentation part carries the data unit identifier in octets n and n+1, the segment offset in octets n+2 and n+3 and the total length in octets n+4 and n+5. The options part runs from octet n+6 through p, and the data from octet p+1 through z.

The RFC presents a specific method for addressing in the Internet environment that is consistent with the international standardized NSAP addresses, which are otherwise discussed in the ISO documents it references.
sections.plainLanguage: The address is not a separate header but two fields inside the CLNP header: first the destination, then the source, each with a length octet in front of it.

sections.title: The Structure of an ISO IP Address
sections.content:
The Authority and Format Identifier (AFI) is one octet and specifies an ISO-6523-ICD assignment, and that the Domain Specific Part of the address is based on binary. The AFI octet uses the value 47. The ISO-6523-ICD format is used to emphasize that this is an administrative assignment; an ISO Data Country Code would be possible, but could be misleading given the far-flung geographical extent of the Internet.

As the ISO addressing standard requires, the next two octets specify the Initial Domain Identifier. This two-octet value is the International Code Designator assigned to the Internet, 0006. The remainder of the address is the Domain Specific Part, which is assigned by the Internet administration, considered to be an addressing domain. There is no particular relationship required between addressing domains and routing domains: although the Internet is a single addressing domain, it is expected to consist of multiple routing domains.

The Domain Specific Part specifies a one-octet version number, a two-octet global area number, a two-octet routing domain number, a variable-length padding field, a variable-length IGP specific part, and a one-octet selector field. The version number allows for future extensions and must contain the value 02. The global area number and routing domain number allow inter-domain routing: the global area number is initially reserved and must be set to zero, and the routing domain number may be set to the routing domain number of any gateway by which the associated host address is directly reachable.

The IGP specific part may contain whatever addressing format the routing domain uses. Padding is used so that the entire address is always 20 octets long. The selector field performs the same function as the user protocol field in the IP header, because the ISO protocol treats identification of the user protocol as an addressing issue and does not allow the user protocol to be specified in the protocol header independently of the address. Assigning the specific routing domain identifiers and the values for the selector field are assigned numbers functions that are outside the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: The address has a fixed shape. It starts with 47, then 0006, then a version number, then a global area number and a routing domain number. The rest is padding, the part the routing domain fills in for itself, and a final byte naming which user protocol is meant.

sections.title: Two Expected Forms for the IGP-Specific Part
sections.content:
A particular routing domain may specify any addressing scheme for the IGP specific part of the address, up to 11 octets long, which is consistent with the maximum address length of 20 octets. It is expected that initially the addresses used in this field will consist of either the current IP addresses or addresses conformant with those in the draft ANSI proposal for intra-domain routing.

For end systems in routing domains that use IP addresses for internal routing, the address takes the form of Figure 3: the AFI, IDI/ICD, version number, global area number and routing domain number as before, then padding from octet 9 through octet 15, then the four-octet DoD Internet address in octets 16 through 19, then the selector in octet 20.

For end systems in routing domains using the address format from the draft ANSI proposal for intra-domain routing, the address takes the form of Figure 4: padding runs from octet 9 through octet 11, and the IGP specific part runs from octet 12 through octet 19, holding a LOC-AREA field and an ID field, with the selector again in octet 20.
sections.plainLanguage: The part of the address that the routing domain fills in can be up to 11 bytes. Two forms are expected: an ordinary four-byte Internet address, or the LOC-AREA and ID fields from the ANSI intra-domain routing proposal.

sections.title: Devices Attached to Public Data Networks
sections.content:
Otherwise isolated end systems, attached to the Internet only indirectly via public data networks, and simple LANs similarly attached only via public data networks, may make use of a separate address format based on their X.121 address, for example the ISO-X.121 address format discussed in the ISO documents the RFC references.

These addresses have to be handled for routing purposes in much the same way as addresses in routing domains that are interconnected to the Internet but use other address formats, such as those specified by national standards bodies.
sections.plainLanguage: A host that reaches the Internet only through a public data network can be addressed by its X.121 number instead, and the Internet has to route for that form the same way it routes for other foreign address formats.

sections.title: Migration to Future Routing Protocols
sections.content:
Initially, routing of ISO datagrams in the Internet may use the first eight octets of the address, the AFI, ICD, version, global area number and routing domain number, as a flat field identifying the routing domain. That implies that if EGP is initially used for routing between routing domains, a new version of EGP may be required to carry eight-octet routing domain numbers instead of three-octet network numbers.

Several efforts were underway to determine the requirements for inter-autonomous system routing and to define a new protocol. One requirement is the need to deal with a very large Internet. It is anticipated that during the lifetime of the addressing scheme described here the number of networks in the Internet will grow to the point where it is no longer feasible for any gateway to maintain separate routes to every network. Allowing inter-domain routing to be done by routing domain number instead of network number is therefore a necessary step in the long term.

It is difficult to anticipate how fast the number of routing domains may grow. If the number of networks grows by a factor of 100, it is not clear whether the number of routing domains grows by a factor of 100 or by some lesser amount. It is possible that the number of routing domains will also grow to a point where it is not feasible for a single gateway to maintain separate routes to each, and the global area field has been provided for that eventuality.

In the long term it will be necessary for gateways to route to destinations in routing domains that use other addressing formats, specified by organizations such as ANSI and ECMA. In that case it will not be possible to ensure that the first eight octets of the address specify the routing domain, and it will therefore be necessary to route based on variable-length routing domain identifiers. It may be assumed that future inter-domain routing protocols will allow either an address mask, specifying which part of an address is relevant for the destinations reachable via a particular domain, or a length field, specifying how many leading octets are relevant. The details of such a protocol are beyond the scope of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The first eight bytes are enough to say which routing domain a destination belongs to, so routing between domains can work from those bytes alone. Later, when gateways cannot keep a route to every network, and when other address formats have to be routed for too, the scheme has room for longer identifiers and for a second grouping level.

fields.name: AFI
fields.desc: Octet 1; the value 47, an ISO-6523-ICD assignment.

fields.name: IDI / ICD
fields.desc: Octets 2 and 3; the International Code Designator assigned to the Internet.

fields.name: Version Number
fields.desc: Octet 4; the value 02, reserved for future extensions.

fields.name: Global Area Number
fields.desc: Octets 5 and 6; initially reserved and set to zero.

fields.name: Routing Domain Number
fields.desc: Octets 7 and 8; the routing domain of a gateway by which the host is directly reachable.

fields.name: Padding
fields.desc: Octets 9 to 15; variable in length but always zero, so that the address is 20 octets.

fields.name: IGP Specific Part
fields.desc: Octets 16 to 19; here the four-octet DoD Internet address.

fields.name: Selector
fields.desc: Octet 20; names the user protocol, as the IP header's protocol field does.

items.title: AFI
items.text: One octet with the value 47, an ISO-6523-ICD assignment saying the domain specific part is binary.

items.title: IDI / ICD
items.text: Two octets with the value 0006, the International Code Designator assigned to the Internet.

items.title: Version number
items.text: One octet with the value 02, present so the format can be extended later.

items.title: Global area number
items.text: Two octets, initially reserved and set to zero, for grouping routing domains later.

items.title: Routing domain number
items.text: Two octets naming the routing domain, which is what inter-domain routing works from.

items.title: Padding
items.text: Variable length and always zero, so that the whole address is 20 octets.

items.title: IGP specific part
items.text: Up to 11 octets, in whatever format the routing domain uses internally.

items.title: Selector
items.text: One octet naming the user protocol, because ISO treats that as part of the address.
